mainTopic: The two lessons of ״אם המצא תמצא״, and רב's rule on which date sets the value of a thief's payments: its source, its limits, and its fit with רבה.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a challenge about the words ״אם המצא תמצא״. A ברייתא uses them to teach that כפל applies wherever the stolen item is found. The גמרא answers that the verse changes its wording (הִמָּצֵא, then תִּמָּצֵא), so it teaches two lessons. Next the גמרא returns to רב's rule. The קרן is valued as it was at the time of the theft, but כפל and ארבעה וחמשה are valued as they are at the time of the court case. רב learns this from the word ״חיים״: 'revive' the קרן at its theft-time value. רב ששת challenges רב from two ברייתות about a thief who fattened a lean animal or made a fat animal lean. The גמרא explains both as special cases, and limits רב's rule to rises and drops in market price. To keep רב from arguing with רבה, the גמרא says רב meant an item that dropped in value. The amud ends as רבי חנינא begins a ברייתא supporting רב, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The same verse is needed to teach where the stolen item is found
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא uses ״אם המצא תמצא״ to teach that כפל applies wherever the stolen item is found, not only in the thief's hand. This seems to use up the verse that was just used for another lesson.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'his hand' only covers an item found in his hand. How do we know the same law applies to his roof, his yard and his enclosure? The verse says 'if it shall surely be found', meaning anywhere.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to challenge the earlier lesson, since this ברייתא needs the same doubled words ״אם המצא תמצא״ for a different teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse mentions 'in his hand', which might suggest that only an item found on the thief's body counts. The ברייתא uses the doubled verb to stretch the law to any of his property. If the doubled verb is used for that, it seems it cannot also teach that a thief pays כפל without a false oath.

keyTerms.meaning: I would only know (this case) — a ברייתא's way of starting to widen a law
his enclosure (a fenced area outside the house)

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא itself is not arguing with anyone. It becomes a challenge only because the גמרא already used the same words ״אם המצא תמצא״ for a different lesson just before this.

phrases.english: I have only his hand,
his roof, his yard, and his enclosure — from where do we know?
The verse states:
'If it shall surely be found' — in any place!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא יָדוֹ, גַּגּוֹ חֲצֵירוֹ וְקַרְפֵּיפוֹ מִנַּיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a challenge from just before this section: the doubled verb was already used to teach כפל without an oath.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier lesson that ״אם המצא תמצא״ teaches that a thief pays כפל even without a false oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One verse should not carry two separate lessons. If the doubled verb teaches 'any place', it cannot also teach the oath lesson.

steps.title: The verse changes its wording, so it teaches two lessons
steps.stepSummary: If only one lesson were meant, the verse would have repeated the same form twice. Because it switches from הִמָּצֵא to תִּמָּצֵא, we learn both lessons.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the verse could have said ״הִמָּצֵא הִמָּצֵא״ or ״תִּמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא״. Since the verse changed the form, learn two lessons from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The change in wording inside the doubled verb is extra, and that extra teaches a second lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plain doubling would teach one thing. The Torah went further and used two different forms of the verb. That change is read as a second hint, so both 'any place' and 'even without an oath' come from these words.
steps.whatToRemember: ״אם המצא תמצא״ teaches two things because of its changed wording: כפל applies wherever the stolen item is found, and כפל applies even without a false oath.

phrases.english: If so, let the verse say
either 'himmatze himmatze'
or 'timmatze timmatze';
since the verse varied its wording, learn two things from it.

steps.terutzResolutionType: An extra detail in the verse supports a second lesson.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The doubled verb gives room for only one lesson.
steps.terutzMaskana: The change of verb form is an extra hint, so the verse teaches both lessons.

steps.title: רב: which date sets the value of each payment
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that the קרן is figured by the item's value at the time of the theft. כפל and ארבעה וחמשה are figured by its value at the time of the court case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the statement itself. רב said: the principal is paid by its value when he stole it. Double payment and fourfold or fivefold payment are paid by its value at the time he stands in court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns back to a statement of רב that came up earlier, and now studies it directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The value of a stolen item can change between the theft and the trial. רב splits the payment. The basic return (קרן) uses the old value from the time of the theft. The fine parts (כפל, and ארבעה וחמשה for a slaughtered or sold ox or sheep) use the value at the time of the trial.

keyTerms.meaning: (back to) the matter itself — the גמרא returns to a statement quoted earlier
principal — paying back the basic value of what was stolen
as it was when he stole it
fourfold and fivefold payment (for a stolen sheep or ox that was slaughtered or sold)
the time of standing in judgment

steps.confusionAlert: רב does not use one date for everything. The קרן goes by the time of the theft, but the extra payments go by the time of the trial.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next question: what source does רב have for valuing the קרן by the time of the theft?

phrases.english: The matter itself: Rav said:
The principal — according to its value when he stole it.
Double payment
and fourfold and fivefold payment —
according to the time of standing in judgment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the verse discussion and returns to רב's statement quoted earlier.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קרן is valued as at the time of the theft; כפל and ארבעה וחמשה are valued as at the time of the trial.

steps.title: Asking for רב's source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רב learns his rule.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for רב's source. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's split between the two payments needs a basis. The question is mainly about why the קרן goes by the time of the theft.

phrases.english: What is Rav's reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule stated in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The verse behind רב's rule on when each payment is valued.

steps.title: The word 'alive' tells us to value the קרן at the time of the theft
steps.stepSummary: The verse puts ״גניבה״ and ״חיים״ together. Since the extra word 'alive' is not needed for the story, it teaches us to 'revive' the קרן at its value from the time of the theft.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says 'theft' and 'alive'. Why does the Torah say 'alive' about the theft? To teach: bring the principal back to life, as it was when he stole it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב learns his rule from the word ״חיים״ in the verse about the theft.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse describes the stolen item as found 'alive'. The גמרא reads this as an instruction to 'revive' the קרן: pay it as the item was, alive and whole, at the time of the theft. Even if it later lost value or died, the קרן still follows its earlier value.

keyTerms.meaning: bring it to life / revive it

steps.whatToRemember: רב: the קרן is paid at its value from the time of the theft, learned from ״חיים״ ('revive' the קרן). The extra fines go by the value at the time of the trial.

phrases.english: The verse says: 'theft' and 'alive.'
Why does the Merciful One say
'alive' regarding the theft?
Revive the principal as it was when he stole it.
phrases.notes: A play on the word חיים: picture the item 'brought back to life' at what it was worth the day it was stolen.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra word ״חיים״ next to ״גניבה״ teaches that the קרן is valued as at the time of the theft.

steps.title: רב ששת says רב's rule goes against a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת says רב must have said his rule while half-asleep, because a ברייתא rules that a thief who fattened a lean animal pays כפל and ארבעה וחמשה by its value at the time of the theft.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: I say that רב said this ruling when he was dozing and lying down. For a ברייתא teaches: if the animal was lean and the thief fattened it, he pays כפל and ארבעה וחמשה by its value at the time he stole it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת strongly challenges רב's rule from Step 3. He brings a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said כפל and ארבעה וחמשה follow the value at the time of the court case. In the ברייתא, the animal is worth more at the court case because the thief fattened it, yet the thief pays by the lower value from the time of the theft. That looks like a direct contradiction of רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Dozing and lying down. A sharp way of saying the ruling was said carelessly.
Lean or thin (said of an animal).
According to its state or value when he stole it.

steps.confusionAlert: רב ששת is not mocking רב personally. This is the גמרא's strong way of saying, 'This ruling can't be right, because a ברייתא says otherwise.'

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said: I say,
when Rav was dozing and lying down
he said this teaching.
phrases.notes: He means רב's rule from earlier: קרן by the value at the theft, כפל and ארבעה וחמשה by the value at the court case.

phrases.english: As it is taught: if it was lean and he fattened it,
he pays the double payment
and the fourfold and fivefold payment
according to how it was when he stole it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: אָמֵינָא, כִּי נָיֵים וְשָׁכֵיב רַב אָמַר לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rule of רב that was just given a source in Step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that כפל and ארבעה וחמשה follow the value at the time of the court case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא has the thief pay כפל and ארבעה וחמשה by the value at the time of the theft, even though the animal is worth more at the court case.

steps.title: The thief gets credit for the fattening he did
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is a special case. The thief can say, 'I fattened it, and you want to take the extra value?'
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: that is because the thief can say to the owner, 'I fattened it, and you will take the profit?!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב. The ברייתא is a special case because the added value came from the thief's own work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's rule is about the item's value changing on its own. Here the extra value comes from the thief's own effort, so it is not fair to charge him for it. רב would agree with the ברייתא in this case.

phrases.english: They say: because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The thief is speaking to the owner.

phrases.english: "I fattened it, and you are taking it?!"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ששת's challenge by explaining the ברייתא as a special case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ברייתא to a special case (the thief's own improvement).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא shows that כפל and ארבעה וחמשה always follow the value at the theft.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only goes by the theft value because the extra worth came from the thief's own fattening.

steps.title: A second ברייתא: the thief made a fat animal lean
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא says that if the thief made a fat animal lean, he still pays כפל and ארבעה וחמשה by the value at the time of the theft. Here the thief gets no credit, so why not follow the court case value?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if the animal was fat and he made it lean, he pays כפל and ארבעה וחמשה by its value when he stole it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new challenge to רב. The 'I fattened it' answer cannot work here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case, the animal is worth less at the court case. רב's rule would mean the thief pays less, yet the ברייתא makes him pay the higher theft value. The answer from Step 7 does not help, because the thief did nothing that deserves credit.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear; introduces a source as a challenge or proof.

phrases.english: Come and hear: if it was fat and he made it lean,
he pays the double payment
and the fourfold and fivefold payment
according to how it was when he stole it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first ברייתא was answered, brings a second ברייתא where that answer does not fit.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that כפל and ארבעה וחמשה follow the value at the time of the court case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The animal is worth less at the court case, yet the thief pays the higher theft value, and there is no 'I improved it' reason to explain this.

steps.title: Making the animal lean is like partly killing it
steps.stepSummary: This ברייתא is also a special case. Weakening the animal counts as killing part of it, so he pays as if the harm began at the theft.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, it is because we say to him: what difference is it if you killed all of it or killed half of it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second challenge. It explains this ברייתא as a special case too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making the animal thin is real physical harm, a partial killing. Killing all of it or part of it is the same kind of act. So the thief pays for the animal as it was before he started harming it, which means its value at the time of the theft.

keyTerms.meaning: What difference is it to me; there is no difference.

phrases.english: There too, it is because we say to him:
phrases.notes: He means the case of the fat animal that the thief made lean.

phrases.english: what difference is it if he killed all of it,
or if he killed half of it?

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ברייתא to a special case (physical harm done by the thief).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second ברייתא proves that payments always follow the value at the theft.
steps.terutzMaskana: Making the animal lean counts as partly killing it, so the thief pays by the value from before the harm.

steps.title: רב's rule is only about price going up or down
steps.stepSummary: רב's rule only applies when the market price rises or falls, not when the animal itself physically changes.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב said his rule, he was speaking about the price going up or down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up and clearly defines how far רב's rule goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ברייתות were about physical changes to the animal, fattening or thinning. רב's rule covers only changes in the market price while the animal stays the same. With this, both challenges fall away and רב's rule stands.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: the קרן is figured by the value at the theft, while כפל and ארבעה וחמשה are figured by the value at the court case. This applies only to market price changes. When the thief physically changes the animal (fattens or thins it), he pays by its value at the theft.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the exact limits of רב's rule. A change in market price is treated differently from a physical change the thief makes to the item.

phrases.english: When Rav said his rule,
it was about a rise and drop in price that he said it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָאָמַר רַב – בְּיוּקְרָא וְזוּלָא הוּא דְּקָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Wraps up both answers by stating the limits of רב's rule.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב's rule (court case value for כפל and ארבעה וחמשה) applies only to market price changes, not to physical changes in the animal.

steps.title: What case was רב talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case רב meant, and suggests an item that was worth one זוז at the theft and four זוז later.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? Suppose at first it was worth one זוז and in the end it was worth four זוזים. Then the principal is paid as at the time of the theft, which is only one זוז.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what kind of case רב had in mind and tries out one possible case. This sets up a problem that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ruled that the principal follows the value at the time of the theft. If the item went up from one זוז to four, the thief would return only one זוז for the principal. The גמרא tests whether that reading of רב can work.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How exactly does it look?
If you say, a first suggestion the גמרא tries out
A זוז, a silver coin (also called a דינר)
The principal, the basic value of the stolen item

phrases.english: What is the case?
If we say that at first it was worth one zuz,
and in the end it was worth four zuz,
then the principal is like when he stole it (one zuz);

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that רב's rule has been limited to market price changes, the גמרא asks which direction of price change רב meant.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רב's rule apply when the item's value went up, or when it went down?

steps.title: That reading would make רב argue with רבה
steps.stepSummary: If רב meant an item that went up in value, he would argue with רבה, who says a robber who broke or drank a barrel of wine after it rose to four זוזים pays four.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should we say רב argues with רבה? רבה said: someone who robbed a barrel of wine from his friend, worth one זוז at first and four זוזים later, pays four if he broke it or drank it. If it broke by itself, he pays one זוז.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the suggested reading of רב by pointing to a ruling of רבה that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה holds that when the robber himself destroys the item after it went up in value, he pays the higher value. Only if it broke by itself does he pay the original value. So reading רב as 'pay one זוז even though it went up' would clash with רבה, and the גמרא does not want to assume they argue.

keyTerms.meaning: He broke it or drank it
By itself, without anyone doing it

steps.confusionAlert: רבה's case is about a robber who destroyed the item himself after it went up. That is why he pays four. If it broke by itself, he only pays the one זוז it was worth when he took it.

phrases.english: Shall we say Rav argues with Rabba?
For Rabba said:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי מַאן דִּגְזַל חָבִיתָא דְחַמְרָא מֵחַבְרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: One who robbed a barrel of wine from his friend,
at first it was worth one zuz
and in the end it was worth four zuz,
if he broke it or drank it,
he pays four.
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is part of the corrected wording.

phrases.english: If it broke by itself,
he pays one zuz.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the suggested case from step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading רב's rule as being about an item that went up in value
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבה says that a robber who destroys an item after it went up in value pays the higher value. Reading רב as paying the lower original value would put רב in an argument with רבה.

steps.title: רב was talking about an item that went down in value
steps.stepSummary: רב meant an item worth four at first and one later. The principal is paid at the theft value of four, while כפל and ארבעה וחמשה follow the court-time value.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: when רב said his rule, he meant a case where it was worth four at first and one in the end. The principal is paid as when he stole it. The double payment and the four-or-five payment are paid by the value at the time of standing in court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by moving רב's rule to the opposite case: an item that dropped in value. That way רב does not argue with רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the item dropped from four to one, the thief cannot gain from the drop on the principal, so he pays four. But the extra fines, כפל and ארבעה וחמשה, are figured by the lower value at the time of court. This case does not touch רבה's case of a rising value at all.

keyTerms.meaning: They say, an unnamed answer in the גמרא
According to the value at the time he stole
The time of standing trial in court

steps.whatToRemember: רב's rule is about an item that went down in value: the principal follows the higher theft-time value, and כפל and ארבעה וחמשה follow the court-time value. So רב and רבה do not argue.

phrases.english: They say:
When Rav said his rule,
it was a case where at first it was worth four
and in the end it was worth one zuz;
the principal is like when he stole it,
the double payment and the four-or-five payment
are like the time of standing in court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רבה in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (going down in value instead of going up)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב was talking about an item that went up in value, so he would clash with רבה.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב was talking about an item that went down in value, so there is no clash with רבה.

steps.title: רבי חנינא begins a ברייתא supporting רב
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא quotes a ברייתא about a שומר who falsely claimed a thief stole the deposit, swore, and then admitted. What he pays depends on whether he admitted before or after witnesses came. This is the view of רבי יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא taught a ברייתא to support רב: a homeowner (holding a deposit) claimed a thief stole it, swore, admitted, and witnesses came. If he admitted before the witnesses came, he pays the principal, a fifth, and brings an אשם. If he admitted after the witnesses came, he pays double and brings an אשם, and the fifth is covered by the double payment. This is the view of רבי יעקב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts bringing a ברייתא as support for רב. This amud gives only its opening part. The ברייתא continues on the next amud, and that is where its support for רב becomes clear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Admitting before witnesses makes him a confessor, so he pays קרן, חומש and an אשם. Once witnesses have come, he owes כפל as a thief would. The extra fifth is included inside the double payment, not added on top. This sets up the background for the support of רב.

keyTerms.meaning: The claim that a thief stole it
A deposit left with someone for safekeeping
An added fifth paid by one who admits after a false oath

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina taught a baraita to support Rav:

phrases.aramaic: בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁטָּעַן טַעֲנַת גַּנָּב בְּפִקָּדוֹן,
phrases.english: A homeowner who claimed a thief took a deposit,
phrases.notes: The homeowner here is the one watching someone else's item, and he is lying about the thief.

phrases.english: and swore, and admitted, and witnesses came:

phrases.aramaic: אִם עַד שֶׁלֹּא בָּאוּ עֵדִים הוֹדָה,
phrases.english: if he admitted before the witnesses came,
he pays the principal and a fifth, and brings a guilt-offering;
but if he admitted after the witnesses came,
he pays the double payment and brings a guilt-offering,
and his fifth is counted inside his double payment;
these are the words of Rabbi Yaakov.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining רב's case, the גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רב.
steps.raayaObject: רב's rule that כפל is figured by the value at the time of court
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא taught by רבי חנינא about a שומר who falsely claimed a thief stole the deposit (the supporting point continues on the next amud)
